First Conditional Using When

There are different types of conditions in English. Some are possible, others are unlikely, while others are impossible. The first conditional refers to a real condition with a possible or imagined future consequence or result.
When recent technologies in an information system are used, it will inevitably get faster and more accurate.
When this college, for instance, gets the new learning management system installed, we will be able to process thousands of student requests.

The first conditional has two clauses, one is the likely condition and the other is the imagined future consequence or result.

Example:

The company will provide an exceptional reward if we get the sought results of this information technology project in time.

The word if is widely used in the conditional clause to indicate that something can be uncertain. However, we can also use the word when in the conditional clause when we want to state that if the condition takes place the consequence will definitely happen.

Example:

When we get the approval of the planning phase of this information system project by the 20th of June, we will initiate the implementation phase on the 7th of July.

This is the grammatical structure for the first conditional clauses:

When + subject + verb in simple present + complement. (Condition)

Subject + verb in simple future+ complement. (Result)

 

It doesn't matter which clause you use first, but in case you begin with the conditional clause, you must place a comma at the end of the first sentence before the beginning of the second one.

 

Example:

When we buy the two new laptops, the laser printer, and the router, our LAN network will be complete and ready to use.
Functional Language, GET: Uses and Expressions

Get is a very common verb in English and has many combinations with adjectives, prepositions, and adverbs to form different meanings and idioms. Such combinations are widely common in informal conversations and informal writing.
When recent technologies in an information system are used, it will inevitably get faster and more accurate.
Excuse me professor, I got confused.
Could I get some examples about information systems and information technology?

Get + Direct Object

In cases when there is a direct object after the verb get, it can refer to obtain, buy, or receive something.

Examples:

I got your email. (receive)

The company needs to get a new information system.  (buy)

The manager got permission to update the databases.  (obtain)

 

Get + Adjective 

When there is an adjective after the verb get, it describes a change of state or situation.

Examples:

My PC got damaged this morning.

Those systems are overloaded, they are getting slower.  

Those computers are getting older. It’s time to change them.

 

Get + Place

When get is next to place expression, preposition or adverb, it means to arrive.

Examples:

When we get to the office, we need to discuss some issues.

Did you finally get there?

images.text: Student: Professor, can an information system be improved when more technology is applied?

Professor: Of course, David. You know, our society is getting more and more advanced day by day, so this will demand for more innovative information systems now and in the future. When recent technologies in an information system are used, it will inevitably get faster and more accurate. A clear example is illustrated by the hundreds of software packages and communications devices used in transaction, decision and learning management systems. When this college, for instance, gets the new learning management system installed, we will be able to process thousands of student requests and other issues in just minutes and not hours as it is happening now.
Student: Excuse me, professor. I got confused. Could I get some examples about information systems and information technology?

Professor: Okay. An information system is designed to help operative and management staff in the collection and processing of data in order to make decisions, process transactions of any kind, to store knowledge in databases for later retrieval and assist them in performing learning and teaching processes.
Student: I've got it now. What about information technology?

Professor: Examples refer to computers of any kind, network technologies, and applicative software, communications equipment, telecommunication machines, other electronic devices and so on. IT technologies in general.
Student: I can see the differences now. I've got another question if you don't mind.
Student: Does it mean that an information system without technology is unusable?

Professor: Not at all. In fact, an IS can be traced back to thousands of years ago when computers did not even exist. But now our reality is totally different. When using technology in an IS, we will ensure competitiveness and efficiency. I'd say an IS now must be necessarily designed with information technology components.
